cards.title: State an assumption the calculation really used

walkthrough.question: Iron powder reacts with 80.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ copper(II) sulfate solution in a calorimeter, and the temperature rises by 7.5 °C. You calculated ΔH by assuming the solution absorbed all the heat released. State one other assumption your calculation needed. [1]
walkthrough.key_idea: Each number you plugged in hides an assumption; name it.
walkthrough.careful: Name the property and link it to water's value.
procedure: List what you put into Q = mcΔT.
Ask what each value assumed about the solution.
Ask whether all reactant actually reacted.
State one assumption specifically, excluding what the stem already gave.
tricks: Scan your working: m used density, c used water's value.
Exclude any assumption the question has already stated.
if_lost: What value of c did you use, and for which substance?
How did you turn a volume into a mass?
Did every particle of limiting reactant have to react?

1_context.short: A one-mark practical point that follows a calculation.
1_context.why: The mark tests whether you understood what the calculation assumed. Reports say candidates do better when they connect the question to lab experience.
1_context.avoid: Repeating 'no heat loss', already given in the stem; the question asks for another.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.1.4: enthalpy change from a temperature change, with Tool-style evaluation of the method.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books mention heat loss above all. Markschemes also credit density, c and completion of reaction.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Density, c of water, completion, or no side reaction.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Each is what was silently used in the calculation. The answer must be specific: name the property and tie it to the value used.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Saying the water was pure: that misses that c of the solution was taken as water's (19M.3.HL.TZ1.2).
trigger_phrases: density of solution is 1.00 g cm⁻³
specific heat capacity of solution is that of water
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: The answer must be another assumption, not the one about all heat being absorbed.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Vague statements about accuracy score nothing. One named property with the value or comparison scores the mark.

3_novel_application.short: A displacement reaction, yet the same assumptions apply.
3_novel_application.why: The assumptions come from the method, not from the reaction. So a neutralisation, a displacement or a dissolving all share them.
3_novel_application.avoid: Writing something specific to iron that the calculation never used.
3_novel_application.disguise: Unfamiliar metal chemistry suggests a chemistry-specific answer.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Point to a number in your working; what did it assume?

4_command_terms.short: State: one brief, specific answer, no reasoning.
4_command_terms.why: State needs a short answer without explanation. Writing a list risks a contradiction, as reported in similar practical parts.
4_command_terms.avoid: Writing several assumptions hoping that one scores; a contradiction can cost you (17M.3.HL.TZ1.5).
4_command_terms.demands: Give one further assumption made in the calculation.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark for any one accepted assumption.

5_time_efficiency.short: Write one line: the specific heat capacity assumption.
5_time_efficiency.why: The c assumption is the safest and always applies in solution calorimetry. It takes one line and needs no rereading of the stem.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Explaining the effect of the assumption, which the command term doesn't request.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip how the assumption changes ΔH: only State is asked.

6_data_booklet.short: The booklet value of c creates the assumption.
6_data_booklet.why: The value you read belongs to pure water, yet you used it for a solution. Spotting that mismatch gives you the mark.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Thinking a printed value must be exact for the solution too.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Section 1 has Q = mcΔT. The question directs you to section 2 for c, which is water's value.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Water's density, 1.00 g cm⁻³, is NOT in section 1; memorise it.

7_elimination.short: Ignore answers about heat absorbed or pure water.
7_elimination.why: The first is excluded by the wording. The second was reported as what students wrote, rather than saying the solution's c equals water's.
7_elimination.avoid: Answering 'more accurate thermometer': that is an improvement, not an assumption.

definitely_wrong.target: all heat absorbed by the solution
definitely_wrong.rule: The stem already states this, and asks for another.
An improvement is not an assumption of the calculation.

walkthrough.answer: Any one: solution's density is 1.00 g cm⁻³; solution's c is 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ (same as water); the reaction goes to completion; iron or CuSO₄ does not react with anything else.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.1.4 with practical evaluation in Tool 1 style.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books stress heat loss. Markschemes credit solution density and c, and completion of the reaction.

trigger_phrases: density equal to that of water
specific heat capacity equal to that of water
trap_boundaries: If the stem gives no heat loss, it won't earn credit as another assumption.
In open assumption questions, no heat lost is accepted (25N.1B.HL.6220.2).
Saying water was pure instead of naming c misses the point (19M.3.HL.TZ1.2).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Marks go to the named property with its value or comparison to water, not a general statement.

disguises: Two marks for two assumptions in a neutralisation (25N.1B.HL.6220.2).
Container heat capacity ignored (17M.3.SL.TZ1.5).
Reaction details that tempt a chemistry-specific answer.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Point to a number in your working; what did it assume?

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark per assumption, up to the number asked, and contradictions can cost marks.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not describe the effect unless the question asks.

6_data_booklet.hack: Section 1 has Q = mcΔT. Water's density is NOT there. Questions direct you to section 2 for c, which belongs to water.

rules: Rewording the stem's assumption earns nothing.
Improvements are not assumptions.
Exception: a stem without a stated assumption can accept no heat lost.

evidence.note: Accepts density, c of solution, completion, or no reaction with other substances.
Most could identify an assumption such as the solution's c equals water's.
Accepts c, density, container heat capacity negligible, no heat lost, completion.
Lists container heat capacity ignored, density and c assumed same as water.
Most named water's c but said pure water rather than the solution's c.
Many had difficulty stating another assumption; often not linked to practical work.

cards.difficulty_signal: Appears in 2025 Paper 1B and legacy Paper 3. Reports note these parts are often poorly linked to practical work.

cards.title: Heat loss is the big error: say where, how to fix and its effect

walkthrough.question:
Equal volumes of HCl(aq) and NaOH(aq) of equal concentration are mixed in a glass beaker. An alcohol thermometer records the highest temperature reached. What is the largest source of error in finding the heat change this way?
A. Heat taken up by the glass thermometer
B. Random error when reading the thermometer
C. Heat escaping to the surroundings
D. Systematic error in the volumes measured with burettes
walkthrough.key_idea: An uninsulated beaker loses heat, so the measured rise is too small.
walkthrough.question_type: Calorimetry: identify error and its effect
walkthrough.careful: Name where heat goes; never write only 'heat loss'.
procedure: Identify what absorbs or loses heat in the setup.
Compare the size of each possible error.
Name the largest and where the heat goes.
Predict the effect on measured temperature and ΔH.
Suggest a specific improvement, such as insulation or a lid.
tricks: Glass beaker, no lid: the answer is nearly always heat loss.
Heat loss makes ΔH less negative for an exothermic reaction.
if_lost: Is the beaker insulated?
Where can energy go instead of into the solution?
How big is that effect compared with a burette's tiny error?

1_context.short: The standard practical error for any calorimetry setup.
1_context.why: An open glass beaker lets significant heat escape, while burette volumes and thermometer readings are comparatively small errors. The report lists a beaker as a large systematic error.
1_context.avoid: Choosing the burette because 'systematic' sounds serious (10M.1.HL.TZ1.40).
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.1.4: determining heat change from temperature change, assessed with experimental evaluation.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books say heat is lost. Exams want where it goes, its effect on ΔH and a specific improvement.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Heat loss to surroundings is largest: C.
2_markscheme_logic.why: This error is much larger than instrument precision in this setup. Markschemes elsewhere also require naming the route or the object losing heat.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Writing just 'heat loss' in written papers; 25N.1B.HL.6208.2 does not accept it alone.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: In written answers, 'heat loss' alone gets no mark; name its source or route.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: C is the tempting answer and correct here. Written versions need the extra detail on where heat is lost.

3_novel_application.short: Thermometer and burette details act as decoys.
3_novel_application.why: Listing named instruments directs you to instrument errors. Yet a lid-free beaker exposes the solution, so the setup description matters more than the tools.
3_novel_application.avoid: Calling any thermometer reading a major error; the report treats these as minor.
3_novel_application.disguise: Technical error vocabulary makes smaller errors sound more serious.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask: is the container insulated? If not, heat loss wins.

4_command_terms.short: An MCQ stem comparing sizes of errors.
4_command_terms.why: The question compares error sizes rather than identifying an error type. All four are real, so choose the biggest, not merely a true one.
4_command_terms.avoid: Stopping at the first true statement.
4_command_terms.demands: Choose the largest source of error.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: All or nothing: all four are real errors, and only the biggest scores.

5_time_efficiency.short: Spot the uninsulated beaker, then answer.
5_time_efficiency.why: A quick look at the container decides it. Written parts extend this with the effect and a fix, so memorise that chain.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Calculating burette uncertainties in an MCQ.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not compare numeric uncertainties for this kind of question.

6_data_booklet.short: No section helps; this is practical knowledge.
6_data_booklet.why: Experimental error patterns aren't printed in the sections supplied. You have to carry them from lab experience.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Hunting for uncertainty values in the booklet.
6_data_booklet.pattern: No table applies; reason from the setup.
6_data_booklet.memorise: NOT in the booklet: heat loss lowers the measured ΔT and makes exothermic ΔH less negative.

7_elimination.short: Tiny instrument and glass effects cannot beat open-air loss.
7_elimination.why: Thermometer heat capacity and burette errors are small in this setup, and a reading error is small too. The open beaker's heat loss remains the main one.
7_elimination.avoid: Assuming the word 'systematic' must make D the largest.

definitely_wrong.rule: A thermometer's heat uptake is tiny in an open beaker setup.
A reading error is small compared with heat escaping.
Burettes are precise; their error is small here.

walkthrough.answer: C. Heat loss to the surroundings from the uninsulated beaker is much the largest error, far greater than thermometer or burette errors.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.1.4 with practical evaluation.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books stop at heat loss. Marks require location, direction of effect and a precise improvement.

trigger_phrases: loss of heat from metal during transfer
loss of heat from beaker to surroundings
using polystyrene cup or a lid
trap_boundaries: 'Heat loss' alone is not accepted (25N.1B.HL.6208.2).
An error giving the opposite effect is not accepted (25N.1B.HL.6208.2).
Water bath and closed system not accepted as fixes (25N.1B.HL.6220.2).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial credit names heat loss. Full credit adds the location, effect on the value and a specific fix.

disguises: Metal moved between beakers, losing heat in transit.
A smaller measured rise in a thermometric titration (17M.3.SL.TZ1.5).
Comparison of two students' apparatus (25N.1B.HL.6220.2).
3_novel_application.heuristic: Follow the heat: where can it escape, and when?

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Written: one mark per specific point; two-mark items need two distinct sources. Do not repeat a point.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not list several irrelevant errors (14M.2.SL.TZ1.1); the mark goes to relevant ones.

6_data_booklet.hack: Practical errors are NOT in the booklet. Memorise the chain: loss, lower ΔT, less exothermic.

rules: An error that would make ΔH larger cannot explain a low exothermic value.
Instrument error options lose to heat loss in open containers.
Exception: with very small temperature changes, the percentage error from the thermometer also becomes large.

evidence.note: Heat loss chosen as the largest error.
Rejects 'heat loss' alone and an error giving the opposite effect.
Accepts improved insulation; rejects a water bath and closed/isolated system.
Heat loss gives a smaller rise; fixes are polystyrene cup, insulation, lid.
Heat loss makes ΔH lower, less negative.
Heat loss was common, but many did not say how to prevent it by insulation.
Most said heat loss but added irrelevant errors.
78% saw that a beaker neutralisation has a large systematic error.

cards.difficulty_signal: Findings: students recognise heat loss well (May 2015). Marks now go on specificity: 2025 markschemes reject the bare phrase.

cards.title: Deduce exothermic or endothermic from what heating does

walkthrough.question: Hydrated cobalt(II) ions and chloride ions are at equilibrium: [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺(aq, pink) + 4Cl⁻(aq) ⇌ [CoCl₄]²⁻(aq, blue) + 6H₂O(l). A pink equilibrium mixture turns purplish-blue when warmed. Deduce, with a reason, whether forming [CoCl₄]²⁻ is exothermic or endothermic. [1]
walkthrough.key_idea: Heating favours the endothermic direction; the colour shows which way it shifted.
walkthrough.question_type: Equilibrium shift on heating: deduce exo or endo
walkthrough.careful: Give both the classification and the shift; one alone scores nothing.
procedure: Match the observed colour change to one side of the equation.
Decide which direction the equilibrium shifted.
Heating favours the endothermic direction.
State the classification and the shift together.
tricks: Colour towards products means the forward reaction was favoured.
Cooling works the other way: favours the exothermic direction.
if_lost: Which side of the equation is blue?
Which way did the equilibrium move on warming?
Which direction does added heat favour in general?

1_context.short: Direction of energy transfer, tested through a colour observation.
1_context.why: This links R1.1.2 to equilibrium. The sign of the reaction is deduced from a shift, which is a common way that exams use energy direction.
1_context.avoid: Reasoning from warming itself: the mixture was heated from outside, not by the reaction.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.1.2: reactions are endothermic or exothermic, by direction of energy transfer.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books teach exothermic through thermometer readings. Here no temperature change is measured; a colour shift carries the information.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Endothermic and shifts right: both needed for one mark.
2_markscheme_logic.why: The single mark needs the conclusion and its reason, linked by AND. The forward reaction absorbs the added heat, so that is why it is favoured.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Writing just 'endothermic': the question asks for a reason, and the mark is for both.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: The classification without the shift or forward-favoured reason does not meet the AND requirement.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Conclusion alone earns nothing. The conclusion plus the shift earns the single mark.

3_novel_application.short: A cobalt colour change disguises an energy-direction question.
3_novel_application.why: The complex looks like transition metal chemistry, but no ligand theory is needed. Only the colour-to-side match and the rule on heating matter.
3_novel_application.avoid: Explaining the colours with d-orbital ideas.
3_novel_application.disguise: A transition-metal complex and colours suggest a different topic.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Hot favours endothermic. Which way did it go?

4_command_terms.short: Deduce, giving a reason: conclusion and reason both.
4_command_terms.why: Deduce means reach a conclusion from the data. 'Giving a reason' is why the markscheme links both points with AND.
4_command_terms.avoid: Giving a Le Chatelier statement without saying which way this equilibrium moved.
4_command_terms.demands: Conclude exo or endo from the colour shift, and give the reason.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark for the conclusion and the reason together.

5_time_efficiency.short: One line: endothermic, because the equilibrium shifts right.
5_time_efficiency.why: The mark needs two facts, not a paragraph. Writing more wastes time and risks a statement that contradicts the point you just made.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Drawing energy profiles or discussing rates.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip explanations of colours and rate effects.

6_data_booklet.short: No section helps; the rule is memorised.
6_data_booklet.why: The sections supplied contain no statement of how temperature affects equilibrium. That rule must come from memory and from R2.3.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Reaching for ΔG or K equations; no values are given.
6_data_booklet.pattern: No table applies; deduce from the observation.
6_data_booklet.memorise: NOT in the booklet: raising temperature favours the endothermic direction.

7_elimination.short: Exothermic is out: heating moved it to the blue side.
7_elimination.why: Heating an exothermic forward reaction would shift it left, keeping pink. The observed blue shift rules that out without any numbers.
7_elimination.avoid: Thinking warmed means the reaction itself gives out heat.

definitely_wrong.rule: Heating would shift an exothermic forward reaction left, not towards blue.

definitely_wrong.target: a conclusion with no shift stated
definitely_wrong.rule: The mark needs the reason as well.

walkthrough.answer: Endothermic, because the equilibrium shifts to the right on heating (the forward reaction is favoured and removes the added heat).

1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.1.2 with a link to equilibrium in R2.3.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books present ΔH first and predict shifts. Exams can reverse it: observe a shift and deduce the sign.

trap_boundaries: AND means both parts are required for the single mark.
A temperature fall that shifts left means the forward reaction is endothermic (17M.2.SL.TZ2.3).
Exothermic forward: temperature rise shifts it left and K falls (22M.2.HL.TZ2.6).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: A conclusion without the shift scores nothing; both together score the mark.

disguises: Cobalt complex colours.
A concentration graph showing a temperature change (17M.2.SL.TZ2.3).
Solubility rising with temperature for a dissolving with positive ΔH (17N.1.HL.TZ0.19).
3_novel_application.heuristic: Hot favours endothermic. Which way did it go?

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Often one mark for a conclusion and reason together, or two when reasoning is split.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip explanations of colours and collision ideas.

6_data_booklet.hack: The temperature rule is NOT in the booklet. Memorise it with R2.3.

rules: Exothermic forward cannot gain products on heating.
A K value does not change with added reagent, only with temperature (25M.2.HL.6209.2).
Applies to the equilibrium position; do not apply this to rate questions, where k rises with temperature in every case (25M.1A.HL.6213.28).

evidence.note: Endothermic AND shift right; alternatives accepted.
Endothermic: cooling shifts left; K decreases.
Exothermic forward: equilibrium shifts left and K decreases.
Positive ΔH dissolving: solubility rises with temperature; 83% correct.
13% wrongly linked rate constant rise to endothermic reactions only.
